claim: Exhaustion of stem cells is a hallmark of aging.
source: Exhaustion of stem cells is a hallmark of aging.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the Abstract and Introduction, supported by citations to López-Otín et al., 2013 and Wang and Jones, 2011.

claim: In the Drosophila testis, dedifferentiated germline stem cells (GSCs) derived from spermatogonia increase during lifespan.
source: In the Drosophila testis, dedifferentiated germline stem cells (GSCs) derived from spermatogonia increase during lifespan, leading to the model that dedifferentiation counteracts the decline of GSCs in aged males.
evidence: This is stated in the Abstract as a premise for the study, supported by prior literature.

claim: Blocking bam-lineage dedifferentiation under normal conditions in virgin males has no impact on the GSC pool.
source: Strikingly, blocking bam-lineage dedifferentiation under normal conditions in virgin males has no impact on the GSC pool.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the Abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: In mated males or challenging conditions, inhibiting bam-lineage dedifferentiation markedly reduces the number of GSCs and their ability to proliferate and differentiate.
source: However, in mated males or challenging conditions, inhibiting bam-lineage dedifferentiation markedly reduces the number of GSCs and their ability to proliferate and differentiate.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the Abstract and supported by experimental data in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: bam-lineage derived GSCs have significantly higher proliferation rates than sibling GSCs in the same testis.
source: We find that bam-lineage derived GSCs have significantly higher proliferation rates than sibling GSCs in the same testis.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the Abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 5.

claim: Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK) activity is autonomously required for bam-lineage dedifferentiation.
source: We determined that Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK) activity is autonomously required for bam-lineage dedifferentiation.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the Abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 6.

claim: Dedifferentiation provides a mechanism to maintain the germline and ensure fertility under chronically stressful conditions.
source: Overall, we show that dedifferentiation provides a mechanism to maintain the germline and ensure fertility under chronically stressful conditions.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the Abstract, supported by the experimental findings throughout the manuscript.

claim: Adult tissue stem cells typically reside in niches, anatomically defined as microenvironments that support their 'stemness' and promote their proliferation.
source: Adult tissue stem cells typically reside in niches, anatomically defined as microenvironments that support their 'stemness' and promote their proliferation, resulting in some daughter cells that retain stem cell characteristics and some that begin differentiation (Morrison and Spradling, 2008; Blanpain et al., 2014; Spradling et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the Introduction, supported by citations.

claim: Depletion or reduction of stem cells results in tissue atrophy.
source: Depletion or reduction of stem cells results in tissue atrophy, and the exhaustion of stem cell function is a hallmark of aging (López-Otín et al., 2013; Wang and Jones, 2011).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the Introduction, supported by citations.

claim: The stem cell pool is dynamic and responds to insults, including injury and starvation in both invertebrate and mammalian model organisms.
source: The stem cell pool is dynamic and responds to insults, including injury and starvation in both invertebrate and mammalian model organisms (Angelo and Van Gilst, 2009; Tetteh et al., 2016; van Es et al., 2012; Yang and Yamashita, 2015; McLeod et al., 2010; Li and Jasper, 2016).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the Introduction, supported by citations.

claim: Dedifferentiation has emerged as a conserved mechanism underlying the replenishment of the stem cell pool after stem cell depletion.
source: Recently, dedifferentiation has emerged as a conserved mechanism underlying the replenishment of the stem cell pool after stem cell depletion (Merrell and Stanger, 2016).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the Introduction, supported by a citation.

claim: In the mouse intestine, extensive radiation ablates Lgr5-positive crypt stem cells and lineage-tracing experiments revealed that secretory cells dedifferentiate into Lgr5-positive stem cells following this insult.
source: In the mouse intestine, extensive radiation ablates Lgr5-positive crypt stem cells and lineage-tracing experiments revealed that secretory cells dedifferentiate into Lgr5-positive stem cells following this insult (van Es et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as prior work in the Introduction, supported by a citation.

claim: In the Drosophila intestine, complete starvation induces the loss of all intestinal stem cells, and polyploid enterocyte cells undergo a reduction in ploidity (called amitosis) and transform into intestinal stem cells.
source: In the Drosophila intestine, complete starvation induces the loss of all intestinal stem cells, and polyploid enterocyte cells undergo a reduction in ploidity (called amitosis) and transform into intestinal stem cells (Lucchetta and Ohlstein, 2017).
evidence: This is stated as prior work in the Introduction, supported by a citation.

claim: In Drosophila gonads, after forced differentiation of all germline stem cells (GSCs), differentiating spermatogonia revert to the stem cell state and become functional GSCs.
source: In Drosophila gonads, after forced differentiation of all germline stem cells (GSCs), differentiating spermatogonia revert to the stem cell state and become functional GSCs (Brawley and Matunis, 2004; Kai and Spradling, 2004; Sheng et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated as prior work in the Introduction, supported by citations.

claim: Approximately 8–14 GSCs reside in a quiescent niche in the Drosophila testis.
source: In this tissue, approximately 8–14 GSCs reside in a quiescent niche (Greenspan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the Introduction, supported by a citation.

claim: GSCs adhere to niche cells and undergo oriented mitosis, resulting in one daughter cell that retains the stem cell state and remains in contact with the niche.
source: GSCs adhere to niche cells and undergo oriented mitosis, resulting in one daughter cell that retains the stem cell state and remains in contact with the niche (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the Introduction and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: At the 4- and 8-cell cyst stage, germ cells express bag of marbles (bam), which is necessary and sufficient for their differentiation.
source: At the 4- and 8-cell cyst stage, germ cells express bag of marbles (bam), which is necessary and sufficient for their differentiation (Sheng et al., 2009; Gönczy et al., 1997).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the Introduction, supported by citations.

claim: During aging, the population of GSCs declines such that at 50 days of adulthood ~35% of GSCs are lost from the niche and the remaining GSCs have reduced proliferation.
source: During aging, the population of GSCs declines such that at 50 days of adulthood ~35% of GSCs are lost from the niche and the remaining GSCs have reduced proliferation (Boyle et al., 2007; Wallenfang et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the Introduction, supported by citations.

claim: The average half-life of a GSC is 14 days.
source: The average half-life of a GSC is 14 days, and for a testis with 10 GSCs at day 0 of adulthood, there should be <1 GSC at 50 days (Boyle et al., 2007; Wallenfang et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the Introduction, supported by citations.

claim: The 8-cell spermatogonial cyst is the oldest stage still competent to dedifferentiate.
source: Interestingly, these studies revealed that the 8-cell spermatogonial cyst is the oldest stage still competent to dedifferentiate.
evidence: This is stated as prior work in the Introduction, referencing previous studies.

claim: In 50 day old males, ~40% of the GSCs are derived from bam-lineage spermatogonia that dedifferentiated.
source: bam-lineage labeling analysis of 4- and 8-cell spermatogonial cysts revealed that the proportion of dedifferentiated cells in the GSC pool increases with aging; in 50 day old males, ~40% of the GSCs are derived from bam-lineage spermatogonia that dedifferentiated (Cheng et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated as prior work in the Introduction, supported by a citation.

claim: bam mis-expression in the bam lineage effectively blocked lineage dedifferentiation, as there was no significant increase in the percentage of lineage-dedifferentiated GSCs in aged males.
source: However, bam mis-expression in the bam lineage effectively blocked lineage dedifferentiation, as there was no significant increase in the percentage of lineage-dedifferentiated GSCs in aged males, from 3.3% in young flies to 3.6% in 45-day-old flies (Figure 1D,E,F).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 1D-F.

claim: The relative number of GSCs decreases significantly by 10% after 45 days in both bam > LacZ and bam > bam genotypes.
source: To our surprise, we found that the relative number of GSCs decreases significantly by 10% after 45 days in both genotypes (from 10.4 to 9.4 cells in bam > LacZ, and from 7.9 to 7.1 cells in bam > bam) (Figure 1G and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 1G.

claim: Dedifferentiation of the bam-lineage does not play an important role in maintaining the GSC pool during aging under normal laboratory conditions.
source: Nevertheless, although unexpected and contrary to our predictions, our results strongly suggest that dedifferentiation of the bam-lineage does not play an important role in maintaining the GSC pool during aging under normal laboratory conditions.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion stated in the Results section, based on the experimental data.

claim: 6–15 days of protein deprivation causes a 25% reduction in total GSC number.
source: Previous work has shown that 6–15 days of protein deprivation (also generally referred to in the literature as 'starvation') causes a 25% reduction in total GSC number (Yang and Yamashita, 2015; McLeod et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as prior work in the Results section, supported by citations.

claim: The number of GSCs recovered to original levels after 5 days of refeeding on standard food.
source: Furthermore, the number of GSCs recovered to original levels after 5 days of refeeding on standard food (McLeod et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as prior work in the Results section, supported by a citation.

claim: After the 5 day refeeding period, the proportion of dedifferentiated GSCs significantly increased from 4.2% at day 0 after refeeding to 19.7% at day five after refeeding.
source: However, after the 5 day refeeding period, this proportion significantly increased from 4.2% at day 0 after refeeding to 19.7% at day five after refeeding and did not increase further after longer refeeding times (Figure 2A and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2A.

claim: Testes with at least one dedifferentiated GSC fully recovered the pool of GSCs after 3 days, while those with 0 dedifferentiated GSCs required significantly longer, up to 7 days.
source: Comparing testes with at least one dedifferentiated GSC (Figure 2B', light blue line) to those with 0 dedifferentiated GSCs (Figure 2B', dark blue line), we found that the former fully recovered the pool of GSCs after 3 days, while the latter required significantly longer, up to 7 days.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2B'.

claim: Blocking dedifferentiation retards the recovery of the GSC pool in a similar manner to control bam > LacZ testes devoid of bam-lineage dedifferentiation.
source: Indeed, we observed that blocking dedifferentiation (i.e., bam > bam) retards the recovery of the GSC pool in a similar manner to control bam > LacZ testes devoid of bam-lineage dedifferentiation (Figure 2H, compare red to dark blue line).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2H.

claim: Dedifferentiation of the bam-lineage promotes recovery of the GSC pool after challenging conditions.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that dedifferentiation of the bam-lineage promotes recovery of the GSC pool after challenging conditions.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section, based on the experimental data.

claim: There were significantly more GSCs in M-phase in testes from mated males compared to age-matched unmated males.
source: We found significantly more GSCs in M-phase in testes from mated males compared to age-matched unmated males (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The rate of dedifferentiation in control bam > LacZ testes significantly increased from 7.0% at 0 days to 30.8% at 45 days when males are housed with females.
source: The rate of dedifferentiation in control bam > LacZ testes significantly increased from 7.0% at 0 days to 30.8% at 45 days when males are housed with females (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: While the relative number of GSCs is not diminished in testes from mated bam > lacZ controls, it is significantly (18%) smaller in mated bam > bam flies.
source: Moreover, while the relative number of GSCs is not diminish in testes from mated bam > lacZ controls, suggesting the pool is preserved, it is significantly (18%) smaller in mated bam > bam flies (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: bam-lineage dedifferentiation is important in maintaining the size of the GSC pool under mating conditions.
source: Therefore, bam-lineage dedifferentiation is important in maintaining the size of the GSC pool under mating conditions.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section, based on the experimental data.

claim: At 15 dpci, there was a significant difference in clone retention with fewer clones retained in mated testes.
source: However, at 15 dpci, there was a significant difference in clone retention with fewer clones retained in mated testes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E, second set of bars).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: After 4 cycles of starvation, refeeding and mating, there was a significant increase in the rate of bam-lineage dedifferentiation in control testes, from 6.9% at day 0% to 43.9% at day 41.
source: In control testes, after 4 cycles of starvation, refeeding and mating, we observed a significant increase in the rate of bam-lineage dedifferentiation, from 6.9% at day 0% to 43.9% at day 41 (Figure 3A,B,E and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 3A,B,E.

claim: When dedifferentiation was blocked, the relative number of GSCs was significantly reduced by 33% compared to the controls after four cycles.
source: Importantly, when we blocked dedifferentiation, the relative number of GSCs was significantly reduced by 33% compared to the controls after four cycles (Figure 3F and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 3F.

claim: Under chronic challenging conditions, bam-lineage dedifferentiation is important to preserve the GSC pool.
source: These results indicate that, under these chronic challenging conditions, bam-lineage dedifferentiation is important to preserve the GSC pool.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section, based on the experimental data.

claim: After 2 and 4 cycles of starvation and refeeding, bam > bam testes were thinner and appeared to lack cells in intermediate stages of spermatogenesis.
source: Indeed, after 2 and 4 cycles of starvation and refeeding, bam > bam testes were thinner and appeared to lack cells in intermediate stages of spermatogenesis (Figure 4B,D,F) when compared to matched bam > lacZ controls (Figure 4A,C,E).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the Results section and supported by images in Figure 4.

claim: After 4 cycles of starvation, refeeding and mating, the number of gonia was significantly reduced up to 33% at each gonial stage when dedifferentiation was blocked.
source: However, after 4 cycles of starvation, refeeding and mating, the number of gonia was significantly reduced up to 33% at each gonial stage when dedifferentiation was blocked (Figure 4J and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 4J.

claim: After 4 cycles of starvation, dedifferentiated GSCs contribute up to 45% more offspring than their wild type siblings in the same testis.
source: Strikingly, we observed that after 4 cycles of starvation, dedifferentiated GSCs contribute up to 45% more offspring than their wild type siblings in the same testis (Figure 5A and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 5A.

claim: There were significantly more bam-lineage positive GSCs in S-phase and in M-phase compared to bam-lineage negative GSCs.
source: We found that there were significantly more bam-lineage positive GSCs in S-phase and in M-phase compared to bam-lineage negative GSCs (Figure 5B,C).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 5B,C.

claim: JNK signaling plays essential roles in regeneration of numerous organs, including imaginal discs and intestine, and can trigger changes in cell identity and transdifferentiation.
source: An evolutionarily conserved kinase cascade, the JNK pathway plays essential roles in regeneration of numerous organs, including imaginal discs and intestine, and can trigger changes in cell identity and transdifferentiation (Jiang et al., 2009; Bergantiños et al., 2010; Herrera et al., 2013; Smith-Bolton et al., 2009; Sun and Irvine, 2014; Herrera and Morata, 2014; Lee et al., 2005; Gettings et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the Results section, supported by citations.

claim: JNK signaling is detected in the somatic support cells in the testis during protein starvation and contributes non-autonomously to the maintenance of the GSC pool.
source: JNK signaling is activated in a variety of stress responses; it is detected in the somatic support cells in the testis during protein starvation and contributes non-autonomously to the maintenance of the GSC pool (Yang and Yamashita, 2015).
evidence: This is stated as prior work in the Results section, supported by a citation.

claim: After 15 days of protein starvation, 51% of puc > GFP testes displayed GFP labeling of somatic cyst cells, while GFP expression in the germline was observed in less than 11% of the cases.
source: After 15 days of protein starvation, 51% of puc > GFP testes displayed GFP labeling of somatic cyst cells, while GFP expression in the germline was observed in less than 11% of the cases (Figure 6D,F,F').
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 6D,F,F'.

claim: After 15 days of starvation and 5 of refeeding, 82% of puc > GFP testes had GFP labeling of somatic cells, and 55% now displayed germline labeling as well, including GSCs.
source: After 15 days of starvation and 5 of refeeding, 82% of puc > GFP testes had GFP labeling of somatic cells, and 55% now displayed germline labeling as well, including GSCs (Figure 6E–F').
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 6E-F'.

claim: Germline cells acquire JNK activity specifically during the refeeding phase, when the burst of dedifferentiation takes place.
source: These results indicate that germline cells acquire JNK activity specifically during the refeeding phase, when the burst of dedifferentiation takes place (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section, based on the experimental data.

claim: After one cycle of starvation and refeeding, the increase in bam-lineage GSCs was no longer detectable in bam > puc or bam > bskDN testes compared with bam > LacZ controls.
source: Indeed, after one cycle of starvation and refeeding, the increase in bam-lineage GSCs was no longer detectable in bam > puc or bam > bskDN testes compared with bam > LacZ controls (Figure 6G–K).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 6G-K.

claim: JNK pathway activity is autonomously necessary for germline cells to undergo dedifferentiation.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that JNK pathway activity is autonomously necessary for germline cells to undergo dedifferentiation.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section, based on the experimental data.

claim: Dedifferentiation of the bam lineage plays no role in maintaining the GSC pool during aging under standard conditions (abundant food and no females).
source: Surprisingly, through a combination of genetic methodologies, we demonstrate that dedifferentiation of the bam lineage plays no role in maintaining the GSC pool during aging under standard conditions (abundant food and no females).
evidence: This is a primary conclusion stated in the Discussion section, based on the experimental data.

claim: Under normal but stressful conditions such as mating or under challenging conditions such as starvation and refeeding, dedifferentiation is important for both the quick recovery of the GSC pool in the short term and the preservation of the stem cell number in the long term.
source: Instead, we find that under normal but stressful conditions such as mating or under challenging conditions such as starvation and refeeding, dedifferentiation is important for both the quick recovery of the GSC pool in the short term and the preservation of the stem cell number in the long term.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion stated in the Discussion section, based on the experimental data.

claim: bam-lineage dedifferentiation is akin to a regenerative response aimed to preserve the number of gonadal stem cells under adverse situations but is dispensable under optimal life conditions.
source: These results lead us to propose that bam-lineage dedifferentiation is akin to a regenerative response aimed to preserve the number of gonadal stem cells under adverse situations but is dispensable under optimal life conditions.
evidence: This is a model proposed in the Discussion section, based on the experimental data.

claim: Spermatogonial cysts can fragment and the liberated germ cells migrate back to the niche to become functional GSCs.
source: Furthermore, our results suggest that spermatogonial cysts can fragment and the liberated germ cells migrate back to the niche to become functional GSCs, similar what was observed upon regeneration of the germline after GSC depletion (Figure 7 and [Brawley and Matunis, 2004; Sheng et al., 2009]).
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Discussion section, based on the experimental data and prior work.

claim: JNK activity may be a universal feature of regenerative responses in Drosophila whether it is to reconstruct an appendage or recover a pool of stem cells.
source: Taken together with our results, these studies suggest that JNK activity may be a universal feature of regenerative responses in Drosophila whether it is to reconstruct an appendage or recover a pool of stem cells.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion stated in the Discussion section, based on the experimental data and prior work.

claim: Germline dedifferentiation does not occur during starvation.
source: Similar to our results, two previous studies did not detect bam-lineage-traced, dedifferentiated GSC in the testis during protein starvation (Yang and Yamashita, 2015; McLeod et al., 2010). Therefore, there is consensus in the field that germline dedifferentiation does not occur during starvation.
evidence: This is stated as a consensus in the Discussion section, supported by citations and the current study's data.

claim: Dedifferentiation occurs during the refeeding period with the maximal percentage of dedifferentiated GSCs being observed only after 5 days.
source: Our work shows that dedifferentiation occurs during the refeeding period with the maximal percentage of dedifferentiated GSCs being observed only after 5 days.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the Discussion section, based on the experimental data.

claim: Both symmetric renewal and reversion could be at play in challenging conditions and may underscore why, following one cycle of starvation, the GSC pool does indeed recover albeit in a delayed fashion even when dedifferentiation is blocked.
source: Both symmetric renewal and reversion could be at play in challenging conditions and may underscore why, following one cycle of starvation, the GSC pool does indeed recover albeit in a delayed fashion even when dedifferentiation is blocked (Figure 2B').
evidence: This is a speculative explanation stated in the Discussion section, based on the experimental data.

claim: Transient activity of JNK in germline cells that dedifferentiate could elicit a change in the epigenetic landscape by modulating Polycomb-group (Pc-g) and trithorax-group (trx-g) genes.
source: We speculate that downstream effectors of JNK signaling could be responsible for this increased cycling. The transient activity of JNK in germline cells that dedifferentiate could elicit a change in the epigenetic landscape by modulating Polycomb-group (Pc-g) and trithorax-group (trx-g) genes, as has been shown in several regenerative contexts (Herrera and Morata, 2014; Lee et al., 2005; Roumengous et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation stated in the Discussion section, supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Potential cell reprogramming of dedifferentiated GSCs may 'refresh' a stem cell's genetic landscape, compared with its wild type siblings that may have acquired genetic damage or imprinting.
source: For example, potential cell reprogramming of dedifferentiated GSCs may 'refresh' a stem cell's genetic landscape, compared with its wild type siblings that may have acquired genetic damage or imprinting.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation stated in the Discussion section.

claim: In control flies, there was a significant increase in the percentage of GFP-positive GSCs derived from dedifferentiated bam-lineage spermatogonia, from 7.0% in young flies to 21.6% in 45-day-old males.
source: In control flies, we observed a significant increase in the percentage of GFP-positive GSCs derived from dedifferentiated bam-lineage spermatogonia, from 7.0% in young flies to 21.6% in 45-day-old males (Figure 1B,C,F), consistent with a prior study (Cheng et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 1B,C,F.

claim: GFP-positive germ cells lose bam expression in the process of reverting to a GSC identity.
source: As expected, GFP-positive germ cells lose bam expression in the process of reverting to a GSC identity (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–B'').
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–B''.

claim: At 0 days, the starting number of GSCs was 10.4 cells in bam > LacZ and 7.9 cells in bam > bam.
source: To our surprise, we found that the relative number of GSCs decreases significantly by 10% after 45 days in both genotypes (from 10.4 to 9.4 cells in bam > LacZ, and from 7.9 to 7.1 cells in bam > bam) (Figure 1G and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 1G.

claim: After 15 days of protein starvation, there was a 33% decrease in the relative number of GSCs (10.4 at 0 days and 7.0 after 15 days of starvation).
source: Similar to these prior reports, we observed a 33% decrease in the relative number of GSCs after starvation (10.4 at 0 days and 7.0 after 15 days of starvation) and a full recovery of the GSC pool after 5 days of refeeding (Figure 2B,B' and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2B,B'.

claim: After the 15-day protein starvation period, the percentage of dedifferentiated GSCs did not increase compared to day 0.
source: In accordance with previous studies, we found that after the 15-day protein starvation period, the percentage of dedifferentiated GSCs did not increase compared to day 0 (compare Figure 2A–G and [Yang and Yamashita, 2015; McLeod et al., 2010]).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2A-G.

claim: At day 0, the rate of centrosome mis-orientation was significantly higher in bam-lineage GSCs compared to lineage-negative GSCs.
source: At day 0, the rate of centrosome mis-orientation was significantly higher in bam-lineage GSCs (green bar) compared to lineage-negative GSCs (gray bar).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 caption and supported by data in the figure.

claim: After 45 days fed and unmated, there was no statistical difference between bam-lineage GSCs and lineage-negative GSCs with respect to centrosome mis-orientation.
source: However, in all of the other conditions, there was no statistical difference between these two types of GSCs with respect to centrosome mis-orientation.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 caption and supported by data in the figure.

claim: There were significantly more GSCs in M-phase in both wild type and dedifferentiated GSCs in testes from mated males compared to unmated males.
source: Indeed, in mated males there were more wild type and dedifferentiated GSCs in M-phase compared to unmated males (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Mating increases dedifferentiation of the bam lineage.
source: In a second set of experiments, we addressed whether mating increased dedifferentiation of the bam lineage.
evidence: This is a hypothesis tested in the Results section, supported by the experimental data.

claim: Increased proliferation of GSCs and outcompetition of resident GSCs by dedifferentiating germline cells alter stem cell dynamics in the testis niche.
source: These results are consistent with the model in which increased proliferation of GSCs and outcompetition of resident GSCs by dedifferentiating germline cells alter stem cell dynamics in the testis niche.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section, based on the experimental data.

claim: At 0 days, the number of gonia at each stage is indistinguishable between bam > LacZ and bam > bam flies.
source: At 0 days, the number of gonia at each stage is indistinguishable between bam > LacZ and bam > bam flies (Figure 4I and Supplementary file 3), while as noted above, the absolute number of GSCs was distinct between the two genotypes.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 4I.

claim: The reduced number of gonia in bam > bam testes is unlikely to be a direct result of the bam mis-expression, as the bam-Gal4 line used is only active in the 4- and 8-cell stage, and bam-Gal4 activity disappears once the cells have dedifferentiated.
source: The reduced number of gonia in bam > bam testes is unlikely to be a direct result of the bam mis-expression, as the bam-Gal4 line used is only active in the 4- and 8-cell stage, and bam-Gal4 activity disappears once the cells have dedifferentiated (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an interpretation stated in the Results section, based on the experimental data.

claim: Both bam-lineage-positive and lineage-negative GSCs had equally high rates of centrosome mis-orientation after 4 cycles of starvation and refeeding.
source: Centrosome mis-orientation in GSCs slows the rate of proliferation during aging (Cheng et al., 2008). However, both bam-lineage-positive and lineage-negative GSCs had equally high rates of centrosome mis-orientation after 4 cycles of starvation and refeeding (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, fourth set of bars).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: In some challenging conditions, factors independent of centrosome orientation may regulate GSC proliferation rates.
source: These data suggest that in some challenging conditions, factors independent of centrosome orientation may regulate GSC proliferation rates.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section, based on the experimental data.

claim: At 0 days old, testes from puc > GFP males had GFP expression in a fraction of hub cells.
source: At 0 days old, testes from puc > GFP males had GFP expression in a fraction of hub cells. However, GFP expression was largely absent from somatic cyst cells and the germline, with 20% and 12% of testes, respectively, labeled at 0 days in fed conditions (Figure 6A,F,F').
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 6A,F,F'.

claim: Of the 97 testes scored at 2 and 3 days post refeeding, 17 (17.5%) had germline labeling.
source: Of the 97 testes scored at 2 and 3 days post refeeding, 17 (17.5%) had germline labeling (defined as any GSC, 1-, 2-, 4-, 8- and/or 16-cell gonia expressing puc > GFP).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the Results section.

claim: Of the 17 testes with germline labeling, most (n = 15) had at least 1 GSC labeled as well as various gonia; only two testes had gonia but no GSCs labeled.
source: Of these 17 testes, most (n = 15) had at least 1 GSC labeled as well as various gonia; only two testes had gonia but no GSCs labeled.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the Results section.

claim: One testis at 3 days of refeeding showed a 4-cell gonia labeled with puc > GFP that appeared to fragment into a 3-cell gonia and a GSC at the niche.
source: In support of our model that spermatogonia fragment and revert to the GSC state after autonomous JNK activation, we observed one testis at 3 days of refeeding where a 4-cell gonia labeled with puc > GFP appeared to fragment into a 3-cell gonia and a GSC at the niche (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Neither mis-expression of puc nor bskDN appears to adversely affect germ cell differentiation as robust spermatogonia and spermatocytes expressing puc or bskDN survive and continue to progress towards meiotic stages.
source: We note that neither mis-expression of puc nor bskDN appears to adversely affect germ cell differentiation as robust spermatogonia and spermatocytes expressing puc or bskDN survive and continue to progress towards meiotic stages (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Germ cells that successfully dedifferentiate must have increased competitive properties, which are currently not understood.
source: Since germ cells from fragmented cysts have to compete against resident GSCs as well as resident somatic stem cells in order to re-occupy the niche, germ cells that successfully dedifferentiate must have increased competitive properties, which are currently not understood.
evidence: This is a speculative statement in the Discussion section, based on the experimental data.

claim: Mating significantly decreases both male and female lifespans.
source: We note that while mating is a normal physiological event, it is stressful as mating significantly decreases both male and female lifespans (Branco et al., 2017; Fowler and Partridge, 1989).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the Results section, supported by citations.

claim: The Drosophila testis niche supports a somatic stem cell population called cyst stem cells (CySCs) that produces somatic support cells.
source: The testis niche also supports a somatic stem cell population called cyst stem cells (CySCs) that produces somatic support cells, which exit the cell cycle and ensheath differentiating GSC daughter cells.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the Introduction.

claim: Certain genetic manipulations cause all GSCs to differentiate, but upon silencing of these triggers, spermatogonia break apart, migrate back to the niche, outcompete the resident CySCs and become functional GSCs.
source: Certain genetic manipulations (transient removal of responses to niche signals or transient mis-expression of the key differentiation factor bam) cause all GSCs to differentiate. However, upon silencing of these triggers, spermatogonia break apart, migrate back to the niche, outcompete the resident CySCs and become functional GSCs by transducing JAK/STAT signals and repressing bam expression (Brawley and Matunis, 2004; Sheng et al., 2009; Sheng and Matunis, 2011).
evidence: This is stated as prior work in the Introduction, supported by citations.
